issue_context.title: X509 certificates can be easily found by target hostname
issue_context.body:
Given an X509Certificate2Collection and a host identifier, it should be easy to find certificates that would match that hostname under the TLS host matching rules.

---

There are a different aspects or interpretations to this problem:

* Should the matching include wildcard evaluation?  (Probably yes)
* Should the matching consider name constraints by the CAs?  (We probably need more tests here before we can have an informed opinion)
  * Depending on how things are reported, maybe we need both a "using just this cert" fast interpretation and a "using the chain" slow interpretation.
* Should the matching include "the target looks like an IP Address, match `san/[@type=ipAddress]`? ("Yes" if wildcard is yes, since that is matching what SslStream would do.  "Probably yes" irrespective)
* Should there be options for most of these things?
* Should there be an option for "only test in the SAN extension?" (with no Subject/CN fallback)?
* Should we make it easier to ask if a cert is valid for a purpose?
  * Should that have an option of "require EKU"?  (Yeah, probably, since things like RFC3161 claim enforcement of that)
* Should we make an accelerator for TLS-Server-purpose+this host?
  * The original thought that prompted this was a new find type for X509Certificate2Collection.Find... so... maybe :smile:.

---

```C#
sslServerOptions.ServerCertificateSelectionCallback =
    (sender, hostName) => _cuMy.Certificates.First(c => c.IsValidForTls(hostName);
```

Though that's possibly over-specialization on the instance.  `_cuMy.Certificates.Find(X509FindType.FindTlsServerCertificate, hostName, validOnly: whatever).First()` might be more reasonable (note that both examples are bad in practice because of how much finalization they create)

---

This might just be the X509Certificate2::IsMatchForHostName from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/28771 plus a similar `X509Certificate2::IsValidForPurpose(oid, bool requireEku)`, and possibly the ease of use unifier as a collection Find option.

@jeffhandley do you think this will still land in .NET 7?

X509Certificate2Collection.Find has some quirks around certificate cloning (it returns all new objects, not a filtered collection), making it a non-ideal API.

The API proposal in #22699 includes adding a `MatchesHostname` to X509Certificate2, which addresses the hardest part of this feature request.

review_comments:
Other testing opportunities:

1. No tests for IPv6 matches. I think it would be worthwhile to have at least one test for sanity's sake.
2. No tests for IP, either v4 or v6, in CN where there is no SAN at all. EDIT: this is maybe a "nit" since CN matching is character-for-character.

What do you think about tests for invalid data for a DNSName or IPAddress?

1. IPAddress that is an OCTET STRING that is not 4 or 16 bytes in length. (Looking for a test for the `Cryptography_X509_SAN_UnknownIPAddressSize` error)
2. A DNSName that is not an IA5String.

Would that lazily throw during enumeration, or is it validated up-front? I don't have strong opinions one way or the other what it does, but I'd be interested to know the behavior.
Apparently it was the case an invalid IA5 was a Decode failure and bad ipAddress length was a late failure.  Made them both be failures in Decode

6125 says "Client MUST NOT seek a match for a reference identifier of CN-ID if the presented identifiers include a DNS-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID"

Even though we don't support `uniformResourceIdentifier` or `otherName` with `SRVName`... we'll end up falling back to the CN if one of those is present in the SAN even without a `dnsName`. If I parsed the RFC correctly, we probably shouldn't.

That's a fair bit of an edge case, but would be interested in your thoughts.

In 6.2.1:

> o  If a server for the application service type is typically
>       discovered by means of DNS SRV records, then the list SHOULD
>       include an SRV-ID.
> 
>    o  If a server for the application service type is typically
>       associated with a URI for security purposes (i.e., a formal
>       protocol document specifies the use of URIs in server
>       certificates), then the list SHOULD include a URI-ID.

As far as I can tell, the generalized routine in OpenSSL https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/cac250755efd0c40cc6127a0e4baceb8d226c7e3/crypto/x509/v3_utl.c#L876 doesn't care about SRV or URI.  I'm pretty sure Windows doesn't care either, but it's hard to find at the moment.

I can certainly add to the docs that we don't consider SRV-ID or URI-ID values.
I suppose it's not really worth actioning, it just seemed like a slight deviation from the intention of the RFC, but, if everyone else does it.. 🤷.
It was a good observation.  I added some tests and updated the docs.

I think this could use a comment something of the affect of "X500RelativeDistinguishedName ensures the ASN.1 is already valid, so we don't need to check for trailing data"

Assuming I am right about that.

Is there a chance this will return a strongly typed `X509SubjectAlternativeNameExtension`? Could this do an `is X509SubjectAlternativeNameExtension` check before creating and copying in to a new instance?

No, `Pal.Extensions` always returns untyped extensions, then X509Certificate2.Extension creates a stronger type, if applicable, and uses CopyFrom to load them in.

Added an assert, though.
Ah, okay, I glossed over `Pal.` in front of Extensions.

Some other test scenarios I would be interested in:

1. Multiple wildcards in the SAN (yes, bogus, in my book, but people will try) `*.*.rambutan.example`
2. Things that are not host names in the `MatchesHostname`. What happens when someone inevitably puts user input in to this parameter?

If I am looking at this correctly, a certificate with a SAN of `*.potato.example` will, I think incorrectly, match `https://dog?example.potato.example`.

Adding a precondition check hasn't made too many things fail... mainly just where there's no SAN being restrictive against what we match in CN.... which is probably OK:

```
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  not a hostname (Unknown, '.') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*.') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  not a hostname (Unknown, '.') (Parameter 'hostname')
  not a hostname (Unknown, '*') (Parameter 'hostname')
  not a hostname (Unknown, '*.') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, '*berry.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  EEP? not a hostname (Unknown, 'cran*.fruit.example') (Parameter 'hostname')
  not a hostname (Unknown, '.FRUit.example.') (Parameter 'hostname')
```

"EEP?" means the test was currently expecting it to return true.

I'm probably not too bothered by that.
I'm not 100% sure how to parse that, but you seem unbothered by the output, so I'll assume it's a Good Thing™.

Saw @GrabYourPitchforks in person (le gasp!) and chatted about this, and we're both good with throwing an ArgumentException if the `hostname` parameter doesn't look like a hostname.

All this really means is that when there's not a dNSName SAN entry (including no SAN extension at all) that the CN match won't match CN="John Smith" against `hostname: "John Smith") or (from the test cases above) won't match literal asterisks in the CN (`hostname: "*.fruit.example" is an ArgumentException, and won't match an unexpanded CN that is a literal match)
Excellent. That pretty much matches how I thought this would work.

I think something missing here is "Is this a valid hostname" check. Right now it takes arbitrary strings that are not RFC 1034 (or whatever RFC you think is worth following). This could lead to confusion in `MatchesHostName` as I described in my comment for the tests.
I would expect an argument exception if the hostname is not a well-formed hostname.
